description: Quasar Technologies is a student-led team building real projects at the intersection of applied AI, mathematics, and scientific research. We focus on genuine, well-executed output from NLP systems to computational research over recognition for its own sake.
summary:
We developed LUNARIS (lunaris.quasacode.com), an interactive web-based decision support system designed to identify optimal landing sites at the Moon’s South Pole for future robotic and crewed missions. Selecting a safe and scientifically valuable lunar landing zone requires balancing conflicting factors, including solar illumination, terrain slope, proximity to water-ice-bearing permanently shadowed regions, Earth communication visibility, and surface roughness. LUNARIS addresses this multi-criteria challenge by integrating the Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (Fuzzy AHP) with the TOPSIS ranking algorithm and high-resolution lunar remote sensing datasets. Mission planners can input linguistic priorities, which the platform converts into mathematically consistent criteria weights to rank candidate coordinates in real time on an interactive South Pole map. This platform is important because it eliminates subjective uncertainty in mission planning, minimizes lander tip-over risks by filtering for slopes under three degrees, and pinpoints strategic zones—such as Connecting Ridge and Shackleton Crater Rim—that maximize continuous solar power and reliable access to lunar resources.
The website is introduced in https://lunaris.quasacode.com
The codebase is introduced in https://github.com/kaanilker/LUNARIS

LUNARIS: A Fuzzy AHP and TOPSIS-Based Decision Support System for Lunar South Pole Landing Site Selection

Introduction

In modern space missions aimed at humanity's return to the Moon and the establishment of permanent bases, choosing the right landing site is one of the most critical engineering and scientific problems determining mission success. The Moon's South Pole is a priority target because it combines two features. Its craters have the potential to hold water ice and other volatile compounds, and its high ridges can receive nearly continuous sunlight. The Moon's rotation axis is tilted only 1.54 degrees relative to its orbital plane, which produces extreme illumination conditions near the poles. Deep crater floors have remained in permanent shadow for billions of years, while the high rims and ridges right next to them can receive sunlight for most of the year (Gläser et al., 2014). Landers and surface rovers that generate power with solar panels therefore need to keep periods of continuous darkness as short as possible.

However, a safe soft landing on the lunar surface cannot be ensured by examining solar illumination rates alone. The rugged crater morphology of the polar regions requires identifying topographically safe areas with low surface slopes (generally below 5 degrees, ideally below 3 degrees) to prevent the lander from tipping over. It also requires optimizing access distance to permanently shadowed regions for scientific exploration, and calculating uninterrupted line-of-sight visibility for direct communication with Earth (Mazarico et al., 2011). In current mission planning, these many conflicting physical, engineering, and scientific parameters must be weighed at the same time. The uncertainties this creates, and the inadequacy of single-criterion analyses, clearly show the need for a systematic multi-criteria decision support infrastructure.

Objective

The main objective of this project is to develop an interactive decision support platform that determines the most suitable landing coordinates for robotic and crewed landing missions to the lunar surface, using a scientific, objective, and reproducible method. In lunar remote sensing, data from orbital missions such as the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) are a critical database. These include high-resolution laser altimeter (LOLA) and camera (LROC) data, which are used to map surface slope, roughness, permanently illuminated areas, and potential water ice reserves (Kalkan, 2022). The Lunaris project aims to turn these multi-layer remote sensing data from raw maps into actionable landing decisions that mission planners can use directly.

Mission priorities (energy continuity, landing safety, proximity to water ice resources, or communication continuity) also vary with the mission profile. The project therefore aims to place the linguistic uncertainties and subjective judgments in expert evaluations into a mathematical framework. When exact algorithms fall short on complex and uncertain real-world decision problems, fuzzy logic offers the solution closest to human reasoning. It models linguistic expressions with membership degrees (Zadeh, 1968). Accordingly, the project aims to integrate the Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (Fuzzy AHP) and TOPSIS methods to calculate criteria weights precisely, and to bring this scientific model into a web-based simulation environment that anyone can access.

Method

Scientific Method: Integrated Fuzzy AHP and TOPSIS Model

In the project, candidate landing sites at the Lunar South Pole were evaluated with a two-stage hybrid Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM) architecture:

Criteria Weighting with Fuzzy AHP:
Five main criteria affecting landing site selection were identified:

solar illumination fraction (benefit criterion)

surface slope (cost criterion)

distance to permanently shadowed regions and water ice sources (cost criterion)

Earth communication visibility (benefit criterion)

surface roughness and crater density (cost criterion)

The linguistic judgments of experts or mission planners on the relative importance of the criteria were converted into triangular fuzzy numbers made up of lower, middle, and upper bounds, and a pairwise comparison matrix was built. These judgments are "equally important," "moderately important," "strongly important," "very strongly important," and "absolutely important." The logical consistency of the judgments was checked, with the consistency ratio required to stay below the 0.10 threshold. The fuzzy weight of each criterion was then calculated with the fuzzy geometric mean approach and defuzzified (converted to crisp values) using the center-of-area method. Normalizing to a sum of one gave the crisp criteria weights.

Ranking Candidate Landing Sites with TOPSIS:
The decision matrix is built from numerical measurements of the five criteria at the candidate coordinates on the Lunar South Pole. It was subjected to vector normalization to remove scale differences between units. The normalized values were multiplied by the criteria weights from the Fuzzy AHP stage to form the weighted decision matrix. The positive ideal solution and negative ideal solution were defined using the highest values for benefit criteria and the lowest values for cost criteria. The Euclidean distances of each candidate landing coordinate to the positive and negative ideal solutions were calculated, and the ratio of these distances gives a relative closeness coefficient between zero and one. The coordinate whose relative closeness coefficient is closest to one was ranked as the most suitable landing site for the given mission scenario.

Technical Method: Web Platform Setup and Development Process

A modern web architecture was designed so that mission planners and researchers can use the scientific decision support model interactively. It was implemented in four stages:

Spatial Data Preprocessing and Structuring: LOLA digital terrain models, surface slope maps, solar illumination series covering the 18.6-year lunar precession cycle, and Earth visibility data were processed. They were converted into lightweight, quickly queryable data structures indexed by selenographic latitude and longitude coordinates.

Development of the Decision Support Algorithm Engine: The Fuzzy AHP pairwise comparison solver, the consistency verification algorithm, and the TOPSIS ranking engine were coded as modular software libraries. They can perform real-time calculations on the client side within milliseconds.

Interactive Interface and Map Visualization Layer: A responsive front end was designed. Users can change linguistic importance scales through dynamic sliders and comparison tables. They can inspect the candidate landing coordinates visually on the Lunar South Pole map and view each point's criterion-based performance distribution.

Domain Configuration and Deployment: The application was moved to a cloud server infrastructure. Domain routing and security certificates were configured, and it was opened to uninterrupted access at lunaris.quasacode.com.

Findings

Product Findings: The Lunaris Web Platform (lunaris.quasacode.com)

The software product developed is the Lunaris web platform, published at lunaris.quasacode.com. The platform turns complex multi-criteria space engineering calculations into an intuitive, visual decision support experience:

Dynamic Criteria Prioritization and Consistency Checking: Through the lunaris.quasacode.com interface, users can compare solar illumination, surface slope, proximity to water ice sources, and Earth communication visibility using linguistic scales according to their mission goals. The system checks the logical consistency of the entered preferences instantly and automatically updates the Fuzzy AHP weights.

Interactive Lunar South Pole Map and Coordinate Inspection: The platform's map module interactively presents high-potential landing regions at the Lunar South Pole with their selenographic coordinates. When a candidate point is selected, detailed information cards show the average illumination percentage at that coordinate, the maximum continuous darkness duration, the local terrain slope, and the distance to permanently shadowed craters.

Real-Time TOPSIS Ranking and Sensitivity Analysis: As soon as parameter weights are changed, the TOPSIS engine recalculates all candidate coordinates. It presents the distance to the positive ideal solution, the distance to the negative ideal solution, and the relative closeness coefficient in comparative lists and charts.

Scientific Findings: Lunar Landing Sites Determined from Parameter Inputs

For three different mission profiles, Fuzzy AHP parameter inputs were defined on the Lunaris platform. The highest-scoring landing sites the TOPSIS algorithm identified at the Lunar South Pole, and their physical characteristics, are presented below.

Scenario 1 (Continuous Solar Power and Landing Safety Priority Mission). Weights: illumination 42%, surface slope 28%, distance to permanently shadowed regions 14%, Earth communication 10%, surface roughness 6%.

Rank 1: Connecting Ridge (CR1 – Point 1; 89.4395° South latitude, 222.8066° East longitude). It ranked first with a relative closeness score of 0.914. A surface slope below 3 degrees provides a safe landing. With solar panels at 2 m height, it has 88.12% average illumination over the 19-year precession cycle, 92.00% total sunlight duration, and a maximum continuous darkness period of 4.58 days, which maximizes energy continuity.

Rank 2: Connecting Ridge (CR1 – Point 2; 89.4399° South latitude, 222.8524° East longitude). It ranked second with a relative closeness score of 0.898. With 92.27% cumulative sunlight duration, 87.93% average illumination, and a surface slope below 3 degrees, it is the second most stable landing location on the CR1 ridge line.

Rank 3: Connecting Ridge (CR1 – Point 3; 89.4516° South latitude, 222.7581° East longitude). It obtained a relative closeness score of 0.882. For solar panels and power towers positioned at 10 m height, it raises average illumination to 92.55% and total sunlight duration to 95.61%, and it reduces continuous darkness to 3.08 days.

Scenario 2 (In-Situ Resource Utilization and Water Ice-Focused Mission). Weights: proximity to permanently shadowed regions 40%, surface slope 25%, illumination 20%, Earth communication 9%, surface roughness 6%.

Rank 1: Shackleton Crater Rim 1 (SR1; 89.7742° South latitude, 203.4952° East longitude). It stood out with a relative closeness score of 0.891. It lies right at the edge of the Shackleton crater floor, one of the permanently shadowed regions with the highest water ice potential. It has a wide corridor with a slope below 3 degrees and an illumination value of 73.70% at surface level (above 80% at 2 m height), which made it the primary target for resource-focused missions.

Rank 2: Shackleton Crater Rim 2 (SR2; 89.6871° South latitude, 197.0983° East longitude). It received a relative closeness score of 0.846. It offers an uninterrupted high-illumination area of roughly 12,000 square meters, with illumination above 70% at the surface and at 2 m height, and terrain slopes below 3 to 4 degrees.

Scenario 3 (Direct Earth Communication and Relay Station Priority Mission). Weights: Earth communication 45%, surface slope 22%, illumination 18%, distance to permanently shadowed regions 9%, surface roughness 6%.

Rank 1: Around the Mons Malapert Massif (approximately the 86.00° South latitude band). It ranked first with a relative closeness score of 0.863. Its high elevation at the South Pole gives it a nearly uninterrupted direct line of sight to Earth. It can also act as a communication relay for the Shackleton and CR1 regions. For these reasons it was identified as the most suitable point for communication-priority missions.

Conclusion and Discussion

The core problem set out in the Introduction was the extreme shadowing caused by the Moon's axial tilt, the mechanical landing hazards of steep crater slopes, and communication interruptions with Earth. A further problem was the uncertainty created by relying on human judgment to decide among these conflicting parameters. The Fuzzy AHP and TOPSIS model developed with the Lunaris platform addresses this need directly, with measurable benefit.

First, an ordinary point on the lunar surface receives about 50% sunlight on average because of the daily cycle. It also experiences freezing lunar nights lasting about 14 Earth days. Against that baseline, the coordinates the model identified in the Connecting Ridge (CR1) region provide 92.00% to 92.27% sunlight duration at 2 m panel height and 95.61% to 95.65% at 10 m height. This yields a relative improvement of 84% to 91% in energy continuity compared with standard surface conditions. Reducing continuous darkness to between 3.08 and 4.58 days significantly lowers the lander's battery mass and heater requirements.

Second, for landing safety, engineering tolerances carry risk even below the 15-degree limit. Lunaris's slope constraint restricts candidate sites to flats below 3 degrees, minimizing the risk of tipping over.

Third, the subjective uncertainties in the decision process are addressed by the Fuzzy AHP consistency check below 0.10 and by TOPSIS's objective closeness coefficients in the 0.846 to 0.914 band. This establishes a reproducible mission planning standard.

These landing site selection findings take on broader engineering significance when combined with current literature on autonomous landing navigation, guidance, and control. For example, Maass et al. (2020) presented the Crater Navigation (CNav) system. It matches craters in camera images during descent to global catalogs and can perform autonomous position estimation even in a lost-in-space condition, down to 350 m altitude. The precise target coordinates Lunaris determines can give such terrain-absolute navigation systems an initial target reference and a local crater map base, improving final approach accuracy. Similarly, Furfaro et al. (2018) showed that convolutional and recurrent deep learning networks that produce fuel-optimal thrust magnitude and angle directly from optical camera images can perform autonomous landing with 98.51% classification accuracy. Lunaris's selection of regions with high illumination rates contributes directly to these optical deep learning networks perceiving surface features without deep-shadow losses. In addition, Zenk et al. (2019) emphasized that simultaneous and perpendicular contact of the landing legs with the surface is vital in PID-based control systems that reduce the descent speed of the lunar lander module. Park et al. (2021) modeled the Moon's orbital and libration motions with sub-meter accuracy using the DE440 and DE441 planetary and lunar ephemerides. Lunaris's slope filter below 3 degrees meets the physical precondition for landing control stability. Integrating high-precision ephemeris data into the system will further improve the accuracy of long-term solar illumination forecasts in future versions.

In summary, the Lunaris project resolves the challenging illumination, slope, resource access, and communication constraints at the Lunar South Pole with Fuzzy AHP and TOPSIS methods and removes uncertainties in mission planning. Through the lunaris.quasacode.com platform it offers an accessible, measurable decision support system with a high level of benefit. The findings show that strategic regions such as Connecting Ridge and the Shackleton crater rim can be prioritized objectively for different mission scenarios. They also show that the target coordinates produced are fully compatible with autonomous crater navigation, deep learning-based guidance, and precision landing control systems, and will directly improve the safety and scientific efficiency of future lunar missions.
